log.user: The year is 1930. Bothe and Becker, in Germany, have found that when the light element beryllium is bombarded with alpha particles from polonium, it gives off a radiation of extraordinary penetrating power, more penetrating than any gamma rays hitherto known. The radiation is not deflected by a magnetic field. What may this radiation consist of? Reason it out.
log.talkie: It must be composed either of particles projected with very great velocity, or of very long waves. In the first place, let us suppose that the particles are projected with great velocity. Then let us imagine an obstacle placed in their path. Some of the particles will be stopped, and the stoppage will be accompanied by a diminution of velocity. Now the diminution of velocity cannot be great, because the particles are stopped before they have traversed more than a millimeter of air, and in air the decrease of velocity due to the resistance of the air amounts to only one-tenth of the initial velocity. Hence the particles must be moving very slowly. Consequently, the radiation cannot be composed of particles projected with great velocity. In the second place, let us suppose that the radiation consists of long waves. Then these waves must be able to pass through matter, and must therefore be able to affect a photographic plate. But they cannot pass through more than a millimeter of air, and they cannot affect a photographic plate at a greater distance than this. The waves are, therefore, extremely short.

log.user: The year is 1930. Bothe and Becker, in Germany, have found that when the light element beryllium is bombarded with alpha particles from polonium, it gives off a radiation of extraordinary penetrating power, more penetrating than any gamma rays hitherto known. The radiation is not deflected by a magnetic field. What may this radiation consist of? Reason it out.
log.talkie: It must be either a new type of electron, or a hitherto unknown form of radiation, or a combination of the two. In favour of the first alternative is the fact that the radiation is extremely penetrating, whereas electrons are not known to penetrate matter to any great extent; and, secondly, that, whereas electrons are always produced when matter is bombarded by alpha particles, no electrons have been observed to accompany the new radiation. The second alternative is supported by the fact that the rays can be deflected by a strong electric field, and also by the fact that they can be absorbed by matter. On the whole, the evidence seems to point to the new radiation being a hitherto unknown form of radiation.
